facts.raw_span: A 31-year-old woman
presents with a 4-year history of recurrent painful ulcerations on both legs and feet
no personal or family history of vascular or autoimmune disease
denies arthralgia or other dermatologic symptoms
takes no medications
denies tobacco or illicit drug use
a reticular purplish livedo pattern is noted over both lower limbs
Multiple chronic, nonhealing ulcers are present over the lateral malleolus and the dorsum of the left foot
white atrophic scars on the lower legs and ankles
thrombophilia, hematologic malignancies, immune-mediated vasculitis, connective tissue diseases, arterial disease, vascular proliferations, diabetes, and medication-induced ulcers
A lesional skin biopsy was performed

concepts.why: The patient's recurrent painful ulcerations, reticular purplish livedo pattern, and white atrophic scars are consistent with livedoid vasculopathy.
The patient's recurrent ulcerations and livedo pattern could be indicative of antiphospholipid syndrome, an autoimmune disorder that can cause vascular thrombosis.
The patient's recurrent ulcerations and nonhealing wounds may be related to an underlying thrombophilic condition, which can increase the risk of blood clots.
The patient's chronic, nonhealing ulcers could be consistent with pyoderma gangrenosum, a rare skin condition characterized by ulcerative lesions.
The patient's livedo pattern and ulcerations could be indicative of an underlying vasculitis, which can cause inflammation of blood vessels.
The patient's recurrent ulcerations and nonhealing wounds may be related to sickle cell disease, which can cause vascular occlusion and tissue damage.
The patient's livedo pattern, ulcerations, and nonhealing wounds could be consistent with mixed connective tissue disease, an autoimmune disorder that can cause vascular and skin manifestations.
The patient's recurrent ulcerations and nonhealing wounds may be related to Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, a genetic disorder that can cause skin and vascular fragility.
The patient's recurrent ulcerations and nonhealing wounds may be related to homocystinuria, a genetic disorder that can cause vascular thrombosis and tissue damage.
The patient's recurrent ulcerations and nonhealing wounds may be related to protein C deficiency, a genetic disorder that can cause vascular thrombosis and tissue damage.
